questions.prompt: You added `"deny": ["Read(.env)"]` to the project-shared settings file, but Claude Code still reads `.env`. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?
options: The tool is ignoring you — run it again
A higher-precedence layer (managed, `--settings`, or project-local) sets the same key, or has it set to an empty list; open that file
Re-save the project-shared file and restart
Delete every settings file and start over
questions.explanation: A setting that does not take is almost always coming from a layer above the one you edited, so the fix is to find and read that layer. Option A is the tempting "edit harder" move the reframe warns against. Option C repeats the same edit at the same layer. Option D destroys working configuration to avoid one lookup.

questions.prompt: The same key is set in the managed layer and in your user settings file. Which value wins?
options: Managed — layer 1 wins over everything below it
User — your own file is more specific
Neither; the tool errors on a collision
questions.explanation: Precedence runs top to bottom, so managed (layer 1) beats user (layer 5) for a scalar key. Option B is tempting because "mine" feels more specific, but specificity is not the ordering. Option C is the array rule, not the scalar one. Option D invents a failure that the top-wins rule prevents.

questions.prompt: Your user file sets `"deny": ["Read(.env)"]`. The project-shared file sets `"deny": ["Read(secrets/)"]`. What is the effective value?
options: The project-shared list replaces the user list, so only `secrets/` is denied
The lists merge, so both `.env` and `secrets/` are denied
The user list wins, so only `.env` is denied
It is an error to set the same key twice
questions.explanation: Arrays merge and scalars are replaced, so both entries stay live. Option A is the tempting mistake of applying the scalar rule to an array. Option C applies a flat winner where the merge means there is no loser. Option D contradicts the collision rule the lesson states.

questions.prompt: You want a rule that applies only to you on this one machine, in a repo you share with others. Which layer?
questions.explanation: Personal and per-machine in one shared repo is exactly the project-local file, kept out of version control. Option A is tempting because the rule is about this repo, but committing it imposes it on everyone. Option C reaches every project, which is broader than asked. Option D means retyping the rule on every launch.
